questions.question: Explain how economic changes drove urbanisation in South Africa from 1867 to the 1940s.
questions.expected_answer: Before the mineral revolution towns were small trading, administrative and farming centres and most people were rural. Diamonds at Kimberley from 1867 and gold on the Witwatersrand from 1886 created fast-growing towns; Johannesburg grew from a mining camp in 1886 to the largest city in southern Africa within a generation. The mines relied on African migrant workers in compounds and hostels, and railways linking ports and mines helped Durban and Cape Town grow. Manufacturing expanded, especially during and after the Second World War, when local factories replaced imports, drawing African families to settle permanently in the 1940s; housing shortages led to informal settlements and land occupations such as James Mpanza's near Orlando in 1944. Poor white farmers also moved to the cities. Many white voters feared African urbanisation because of job competition and the threat to white political control, which shaped later laws.

questions.question: Describe the laws used to control African urbanisation under segregation and apartheid.
questions.expected_answer: The Natives (Urban Areas) Act of 1923 set up separate locations and controlled residence, based on the view that Africans should be in towns only to serve white needs. After 1948 influx control limited the number of Africans in urban areas: from 1952 African men, and later women, had to carry a reference book or dompas, and Section 10 allowed residence beyond 72 hours only to those born and continuously resident there, lawfully resident for 15 years, working for one employer for 10 years, their dependants, or permit holders; millions were arrested under the pass laws. The Group Areas Act of 1950 divided cities by race and caused forced removals from District Six, Sophiatown and Cato Manor to townships such as Soweto, Mitchells Plain and Chatsworth. Hostels and limited family housing, and a coloured labour preference in the Western Cape, kept the urban African population small and temporary. Resistance included the women's march of 9 August 1956 and the Sharpeville protest of 21 March 1960, where 69 were killed.

questions.question: Explain the homelands, displaced urbanisation and the end of influx control.
questions.expected_answer: From 1959 the government assigned Africans to ethnic homelands based on the reserves, about 13 per cent of the land, making them homeland citizens; Transkei (1976), Bophuthatswana (1977), Venda (1979) and Ciskei (1981) were declared independent but unrecognised. Homelands were overcrowded and eroded with few jobs, and hundreds of thousands were removed into them from farms, black spots and cities. Displaced urbanisation produced dense urban-sized settlements inside homelands near industrial areas, such as Mdantsane, Botshabelo, Ga-Rankuwa, Mabopane and KwaNdebele, with long daily bus and train commutes, and border industries were encouraged. By the 1980s influx control collapsed because the economy needed workers, people kept coming, settlements such as Crossroads resisted removal and enforcement was costly; it was abolished in 1986 and urbanisation accelerated. In 1994 the homelands were reincorporated; today about two-thirds of South Africans are urban, but the apartheid spatial pattern remains.
